items.title: SECURITY AND PRIVACY CHALLENGES IN AGENTIC AI SYSTEMS
items.abstract: Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems can plan multi-step tasks, use external tools, retrieve information, andtake actions with limited human intervention. These capabilities create security and privacy risks beyond those found inconventional question-answering systems. An agent may encounter malicious instructions in retrieved content, misuse anauthorized tool, expose confidential context, retain unnecessary personal data, or continue a harmful action through a chain ofotherwise ordinary steps. This paper presents a risk-aware framework for analysing these challenges across the agent lifecycle. Itorganizes the main risks into instruction and prompt injection, excessive agency, insecure tool integration, data leakage, identityand access-control weaknesses, memory risks, and insufficient monitoring. The proposed approach combines least-privilegepermissions, separation of trusted instructions from untrusted data, explicit approval for high-impact actions, privacy-awarememory, output validation, and audit logging. A staged evaluation plan is described using threat scenarios and measurablesecurity and privacy indicators. This paper is a design-oriented study and does not claim experimental results or a deployedsecurity product. Its central argument is that agentic AI should be treated as a socio-technical system whose safety depends on themodel, tools, data, permissions, and surrounding operational controls

items.title: SENSE: A Sensor-Centric Multimodal Evidence Chain for Teaching Evaluation in Smart Classrooms
items.abstract: Smart-classroom teaching evaluation increasingly relies on heterogeneous sensing sources, including classroom cameras, microphones, speech-recognition systems, and learning-platform interaction logs. Existing systems often treat these streams as separate analytical inputs, with insufficient attention to cross-modal alignment, missing-sensor robustness, and evidence-grounded large-language-model reasoning. This paper proposes SENSE (Sensor-Evidence Network for Smart-Classroom Evaluation), a sensor-centric framework that organizes classroom evaluation as an end-to-end evidence chain. Visual behavior, acoustic-semantic content, and learning-platform events are aligned in lesson-level time windows and converted into structured evidence packets. Available learning-outcome anchors provide contextual evidence to the semantic evaluator, whereas expert ratings are retained exclusively as external validation references. A DeepSeek-based semantic evaluator then generates engagement, instructional-content, interaction-quality, and teaching-feedback judgments under a fixed output schema. The framework was evaluated using 48 college-English lessons, 48 videos, 48 audio recordings, 4628 timestamped learning-platform interaction logs, and 960 valid student-window observation instances. Compared with a transparent rule-based operational baseline, SENSE reduced the engagement-evaluation error from 12.3% to 5.8%, reduced the content-coverage error from 14.5% to 6.2%, and increased the correlation with the mean expert score from 0.71 to 0.89. Under 30% random evidence removal, the correlation remained 0.80. The results indicate that teaching evaluation benefits from a multimodal sensor-evidence and semantic-reasoning process rather than a single behavior-recognition task.

items.abstract: To analyze factors related to the meaning attributed to police work and understand elements associated with strengthening or weakening the perception of purpose in the role. Method: An integrative literature review was conducted through searches in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, SciELO, and the Virtual Health Library, considering studies published from January 2021 to September 2026 in Portuguese, English, and Spanish. Original studies addressing police officers’ professional experiences were included, considering occupational identity, job satisfaction, work engagement, motivation, organizational support, stress, occupational strain, and work-life balance. Study selection was presented using a flowchart based on PRISMA 2020, resulting in 19 included studies. Results: Findings showed that the meaning of work is influenced by individual, relational, and institutional factors. Professional identity, recognition, organizational support, organizational justice, autonomy, satisfaction, and resilience were associated with more positive work experiences, whereas workload, stress, emotional demands, work-family conflicts, and organizational difficulties were associated with occupational strain and weakening of the bond with the activity. Conclusion: Loss of purpose should not be understood solely as a lack of individual motivation, but as a phenomenon related to the concrete conditions under which police work is performed. Strengthening institutional support, professional recognition, work schedule organization, and occupational health care may contribute to maintaining the meaning attributed to police work and sustaining healthier and more meaningful professional relationships throughout the career. Such measures may reduce the distance between professional expectations and everyday work experiences in diverse institutional contexts and at different stages of professional trajectories over time.

items.title: SFOE Geothermal Workshop 2026
items.abstract: Geothermal Energy: Aligning Research with Project Needs The development of geothermal energy in Switzerland relies not only on the implementation of new technologies but also on a better understanding of the subsurface and its various potential uses. A key challenge is to better bridge the gap between research advances and the practical needs of projects. With this in mind, the second edition of the geothermal workshop organized by the SFOE in September brought together nearly 80 participants from the research community, industry, and public authorities. The event highlighted research efforts, field experiences, and challenges related to project development, focusing on three themes: subsurface exploration, underground heat storage, and next-generation geothermal systems. The first part of the day was devoted to geothermal exploration and developments since the first edition of the workshop in 2024, which was entirely dedicated to this topic. swisstopo provided a detailed overview of the entire process for managing geothermal data from exploration projects supported by the federal government, from collection through quality control (QC) to publication. The resulting lessons learned and future prospects were also discussed. A roundtable bringing together representatives from research, industry, and swisstopo then provided an opportunity to discuss the progress made in transferring research results into practice, as well as the obstacles still encountered—whether technical in nature or related to the adoption of these innovations and their integration into the exploration programs of commercial projects. The discussions showed that new methods can improve geothermal exploration, but that there is no single solution capable of meeting all needs. Innovative methods are particularly useful when they complement more traditional approaches, thereby providing a more robust representation of the subsurface. Similarly, artificial intelligence offers new possibilities for analyzing large amounts of data, but it does not replace the human expertise needed to interpret the results and build a reliable picture of the subsurface. Storing Heat UndergroundThe second section focused on thermal storage underground and its potential to bring greater flexibility to the energy system. The SFOE’s strategic and regulatory perspective was supplemented by several case studies from pilot projects, such as thermal storage in a Quaternary aquifer at theZurich Airport and the project aimed at seasonally storing waste heat underground at the Forsthaus (BE) power plant, which notably allowed for the exploration of various approaches to increase the reservoir’s transmissivity. Practical insights into the environmental monitoring of groundwater in a high-temperature storage system within a geothermal well field on the Empa-Eawag campus were also presented. Finally, the aquifer temperature observatory in Sion provided an opportunity to discuss methods for characterizing and monitoring the thermal evolution of an aquifer on a regional scale, as well as practical aspects related to measuring the effects of thermal groundwater extraction. All of this feedback, particularly regarding environmental monitoring and surveillance, provides an essential foundation for developing the framework conditions necessary for the effective deployment of these storage systems in Switzerland. Next-Generation Geothermal SystemsIn the final part of the workshop, an overview was provided of several approaches to developing next-generation geothermal systems (next-gen technologies). Notably presented were modular closed-loop AGS (Advanced Geothermal Systems) using technology developed by EAPOSYS, as well as the AgenS project in the Upper Rhine Graben, which relies on the development of multilateral wells from a single vertical borehole to reduce seismic risk. Reducing seismic risk is also at the heart of innovative work related to EGS (Enhanced Geothermal System) technology, as illustrated by the Haute-Sorne (JU), as well as the research conducted by the InEarth project to better understand seismicity induced by fluid injections during hydraulic stimulation. Finally, discussions focused on new approaches to heat storage in fractured rocks and low-permeability reservoirs, particularly in crystalline rocks. These concepts rely on hydraulic stimulation techniques similar to those used for EGS systems. An Essential CollaborationThe discussions showed that the subsurface can play an important role in the energy transition, whether for producing or storing energy. To achieve this, reliable subsurface characterization and innovative technologies are required. To harness this potential in a safe, sustainable, and economically viable manner, close collaboration between research, industry, and government remains essential. Sharing data and knowledge will also be a key factor for success.

items.title: Shariah Liability for Artificial Intelligence Errors in Concluding Islamic Financial Contracts
items.abstract: This study examines a contemporary fiqh issue concerning the determination of Shariah liability for artificial intelligence errors in the conclusion of Islamic financial contracts within the banking and financial sectors. The research problem lies in the absence of a conclusive fiqh characterization of the nature of the role played by artificial intelligence technologies in contractual processes: whether they should be regarded merely as rigid technical tools for execution, or whether their autonomous actions may be analogically characterized in light of the rules of wakālah (agency) and niyābah (representation), and the implications of such characterization for determining the party responsible for ḍamān when technical errors or unauthorized actions occur. The study adopts inductive, analytical, and comparative approaches by examining the fiqh rules governing contracts, ḍamān, causation, and tafrīṭ (negligence), and comparing them with contemporary technological functions. The study concludes, among other findings, that artificial intelligence does not possess independent Shariah legal capacity or a separate financial liability, and that its actions remain governed by the nature of the authorities granted to it and the human inputs involved. It further establishes that the machine cannot be attributed independent fiqh reasoning. The study also concludes that Shariah liability and the rules of ḍamān may be distributed among the programming entity, the financial institution using the system, and the human supervisor, according to the relevant criteria of negligence, tafrīṭ, or errors in system design and data. The study recommends the development of regulatory frameworks and robust Shariah guidelines, together with strengthening qualified human oversight to ensure the integrity of financial transactions and compliance with Shariah requirements.

items.title: Síndrome de Burnout em profissionais da saúde atuantes na unidade de terapia intensiva.
items.abstract: Burnout syndrome is an occupational health concern among professionals working in Intensive Care Units (ICUs), settings characterized by complex care and high physical and emotional demands. This study aimed to analyze the impacts of burnout on these professionals and its relationship with patient safety and quality of care. An integrative literature review was conducted using a qualitative, descriptive, and exploratory approach, with searches in SciELO, PubMed, the Virtual Health Library, and Google Scholar. Eligible articles were published between 2015 and 2025, available in full text, written in Portuguese, English, or Spanish, and related to the study topic. The analysis identified workload overload, long working hours, staff shortages, frequent exposure to suffering, and insufficient institutional support as factors associated with burnout. Occupational exhaustion was associated with impaired attention, communication, and decision-making, with implications for quality of care and patient safety. Prevention strategies included adequate staffing, psychological support, professional recognition, and improved working conditions. It was concluded that early recognition of burnout and the adoption of institutional prevention measures are essential to promoting professionals’ mental health and ensuring safe, humanized care in intensive care settings.

items.title: Six domains in pancreatic cancer care
items.abstract: Abstract Pancreatic cancer is an aggressive malignancy with a poor prognosis and complex supportive-care needs. Individualized tumor-directed treatment remains the central axis of care, while evolving nutritional and metabolic status, biliary complications, pain, inflammatory burden, thrombotic risk, and psychological distress may affect treatment readiness, tolerance, continuity, and quality of life. This review proposes the Six-Domain Supportive Care Framework, which organizes 6 clinically relevant and interacting priorities longitudinally around individualized tumor-directed treatment: Cancer Cachexia and Metabolic Derangement, Obstructive Jaundice and Infection Risk, Perineural Invasion and Neuropathic Pain, Chronic Cholangitis and Inflammatory Burden, Cancer-Associated Thrombosis and Coagulopathy, and Psychological Distress and quality of life. We focus on pancreatic cancer-specific evidence across these domains and draw on relevant gastrointestinal and broader oncology studies when direct evidence is limited. The 6 domains also involve longitudinal information from clinical records, laboratory tests, imaging, and patient-reported outcomes. Advances in digital health and artificial intelligence (AI) create new opportunities to integrate these heterogeneous data for risk identification, longitudinal monitoring, clinical prioritization, and clinician-supervised decision support. By linking current clinical evidence with AI-assisted data integration and decision support, this framework provides a clinically oriented perspective on coordinated longitudinal supportive care in pancreatic cancer and highlights priorities for future validation and clinical translation.

items.title: SkillMatch: An Integrated Platform for AI Resume Analysis, Job Description Matching, and Interview Preparation
items.abstract: SkillMatch is a full-stack, AI-powered web application that unifies resume analysis, resume enhancement, job-description matching, cover-letter generation, and interview preparation in a single platform. It is designed to help students and job seekers understand exactly why their resumes may be rejected by Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS) and what they can do to improve them. The work addresses several gaps in existing tools: most candidates do not know why their resume fails at the ATS screening stage; existing tools either give an opaque score with no explanation or solve only one part of the problem, such as a resume builder or a job board; interview preparation is typically disconnected from the candidate's actual resume content; and premium tools that offer detailed feedback are expensive and inaccessible to students. The system combines a React frontend, a Node.js/Express backend, and a PostgreSQL database, using deterministic processing for parsing, grading, and score tallying, and generative AI for rubric-based scoring, skill-gap detection, and interview-question generation. The cover-letter module saves job seekers from writer's block by automatically turning their resume and job-match data into a customized, ready-to-send pitch. The implemented platform completes the main workflow from resume submission to analysis, feedback, and career-preparation support, although AI-based scores vary slightly between runs and scanned resumes are not yet supported. Further testing with larger numbers of users and resumes is required to evaluate accuracy and effectiveness. Keywords— Applicant Tracking System; Resume Analysis; Job Description Matching; Interview Preparation; Generative AI; Cover Letter Generation

items.title: Smart questioning, answering, and clarifying to support adaptive learning
items.abstract: Purpose Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is increasingly integrated into higher education; however, many AI-based systems function primarily as reactive answer generators rather than adaptive instructional supports. This study develops and evaluates smart questioning, answering, and clarifying (SmartQAC), a pedagogically grounded AI-supported learning system that operationalizes structured dialogic scaffolding through questioning, answering, and clarification mechanisms to support adaptive learning. Design/methodology/approach SmartQAC integrates retrieval-augmented generation, prompt-routing strategies, and structured dialogic interactions to promote metacognitive engagement and conceptual development. A quasi-experimental study involving 52 undergraduate students was conducted within a database course as an illustrative domain application. Mixed-method analyses were performed using pre-test and post-test assessments, interaction logs, questionnaires, and interviews to examine learning achievement, learning behaviors, and learner perceptions. Findings Results indicate that students using SmartQAC achieved significantly higher learning achievement than those in the control group. Interaction behaviors within the SmartQAC environment were positively associated with students' learning achievement. Furthermore, participants reported positive perceptions regarding instructional usefulness, autonomy support, engagement, and pedagogical value. Originality/value This study demonstrates how dialogic instructional principles can be operationalized within a retrieval-augmented large language model system to support adaptive learning. The findings provide empirical evidence for the effectiveness of integrating questioning, answering, and clarification mechanisms into AI-supported learning environments and offer practical design implications for future adaptive educational systems.

items.title: Smart Skill Hub: An AI-Driven Platform for Personalized Learning, Career Tracking, And Skill Development
items.abstract: The rapid growth of software technologies has created a significant challenge for students and early-career developers: acquiring technical skills is no longer sufficient without continuously identifying skill gaps, following structured learning paths, demonstrating practical coding ability, maintaining a professional portfolio, and preparing effective resumes. Existing learning platforms generally address individual aspects of this process, resulting in fragmented workflows in which learners use multiple applications for learning, coding practice, resume creation, GitHub analysis, portfolio development, and career guidance. This paper presents Smart Skill Hub (SSH), an integrated AI-powered skill development and career readiness platform designed to unify these activities within a single ecosystem. Smart Skill Hub combines personalized skill profiling, skill-gap analysis, AI-generated learning roadmaps, educational video discovery, coding assessment, GitHub intelligence, AI-assisted resume analysis and generation, portfolio management, analytics, and an AI-based Smart Mentor. The platform uses a modern web architecture consisting of a React and TypeScript frontend, Node.js and Express backend services, MongoDB for persistent data storage, Firebase Authentication for identity management, and centralized Large Language Model services for intelligent features. A secure Docker-based coding execution environment is used to execute programming submissions with resource and network restrictions. The platform maintains a canonical representation of learner skills and profile information so that information can be reused consistently across learning, assessment, resume, portfolio, and mentoring workflows. Resume processing supports document extraction, structured profile generation, interactive A4 editing, multiple ATS-oriented templates, AI-assisted improvement, job-specific analysis, and selectable-text PDF generation. GitHub Intelligence analyses authenticated GitHub activity to derive development insights, while analytics provide learners and administrators with measurable information about activity and system usage. Smart Skill Hub demonstrates an integrated approach to student skill development by connecting learning, assessment, professional representation, and AI-based guidance in a unified platform. The resulting system is designed to reduce fragmentation, improve personalization, and provide students with a continuous workflow from identifying skills and gaps to developing, demonstrating, and presenting those skills.

items.title: SPINAL-CORD Model: Integrating Human and System Factors in Modern Aviation Safety
items.abstract: Classical human factors models transformed aviation safety by shifting attention from individual blame to systemic understanding. Yet the operational landscape of modern aviation has evolved considerably: automation is pervasive, cognitive demands are higher, and understanding of neurocognition and behavioral variability is richer than when foundational frameworks were built. This paper introduces the SPINAL-CORD model, an original safety integration heuristic designed to complement, not replace, established frameworks. The model comprises two interacting components: SPINAL (Skills, Personal Factors, Intelligence, Neurocognition, Adaptability and Resilience, Learning), representing the human behavioral and cognitive core, and CORD (Computing, Organization, Rules, Data), representing the structured operational environment. Together they conceptualise safety as continuously co-produced at the human-system interface, rather than residing in either the operator or the system alone. The paper describes the model's theoretical foundations in cognitive science, resilience engineering, and systems thinking; its relationship to other models; and its practical applications in training, debriefing, and incident analysis. Limitations and directions for future empirical validation are discussed. The model offers practitioners a visual and conceptual anchor for conversations about performance, strain, and adaptive capacity in complex aviation environments.

items.title: Steering an LLM AutoResearch Loop with Domain Context: A Case Study with Vehicle Energy Models
items.abstract: Research Software Engineers (RSEs) often work with Machine Learning (ML) models integratedinto scientific software stacks, and incremental model improvements are valuable but expensivein human time and attention. Our team maintains RouteE-Powertrain, which predicts vehicleenergy consumption and is integrated into RouteE-Compass for energy-aware routing.We investigated whether a Large Language Model (LLM) agent could help accelerate thediscovery process for model improvements by taking on certain elements that are challengingfor us, like context switching and managing limited time budgets. We began with an existingautomated research harness (Andrej Karpathy's autoresearch) where an agent canrepeatedly modify the model and then evaluate against a held-out dataset. This harness foundlarge improvements in our error metrics, but upon further inspection, the winning model wasunusable in our application domain. Specifically, it used unobservable future road network linkstates that are not compatible with our energy-aware route planning application and yielded avery large compute cost at inference time, leading to prohibitive computational overhead forroute planning. We also identified the need for additional agent instruction around logging,single-variable experimentation, token accounting, and trial budgets to support improvedanalysis. We accumulated these discoveries into a modified harness that would guide the agentwithin our narrower optimization space.We then ran two sessions over the same modified harness, each ~50 trials, ~8 hours wall time,~$35 token cost. The first session included our complete modified harness, whereas the secondsession excluded only the domain-specific guidance. Both sessions were then audited in anenvironment where only valid input features were used, for one million model evaluations. Theunguided experiment chose a final model of an ensemble of 75% GBDT/25% CNN and reporteda better overall RMSE score, but when audited, the model performed even worse than thebaseline and took 951 seconds to run one million evaluations (0.95ms/eval). The domain-guidedexperiment produced a 2x128 MLP with a properly constrained feature set which reduced ournetwork link-level RMSE by 49% and completed the audit in 1.4 seconds (0.0014ms/eval).Grounding the agent with explicit deployment constraints ensured that all improvementsremained usable in our application, highlighting that human-in-the-loop domain context is criticalfor this type of automated discovery.We have open sourced the modified harness, along with the archive of the two experimentsessions, with the hope that this will be a valuable resource for other RSE teams whomaintain ML models.

items.title: Structured Knowledge Extraction from Wheat Variety Approval Texts via Relation-Aware In-Context Learning and Progressive Knowledge Calibration
items.abstract: Knowledge extraction serves as a critical technique for constructing domain-specific knowledge graphs and enabling intelligent text parsing. In the vertical agricultural domain, wheat variety approval texts contain abundant agronomic trait entities and their relational associations. Nevertheless, they are characterized by dense domain-specific terminology, the co-occurrence of multiple relations, long entity spans, and mixed numerical and textual expressions, which pose considerable challenges to the accurate extraction of entity-relation triples. Existing in-context learning paradigms mostly retrieve demonstrations based on general-purpose semantic embeddings. The retrieved demonstrations rarely achieve relation-structure matching with query instances; furthermore, LLMs are susceptible to format hallucinations, which limit entity and relation extraction performance. Accordingly, we propose Relation-aware Demonstration Retrieval and Progressive Knowledge Calibration for In-Context Learning (ReCal-ICL), a relation-aware in-context learning framework for joint entity and relation extraction. ReCal-ICL employs RADS, a relation-aware demonstration selector based on hierarchical contrastive learning. Through hierarchical quadruples, in-batch dynamic negative sampling, and a hybrid loss, RADS reshapes the representation space to enhance relational-structure matching between retrieved demonstrations and query instances. In addition, a two-layer output constraint strategy is developed, which integrates prompt-template prior constraints and post hoc result verification mechanisms to jointly guarantee the format compliance of extraction outputs. We conduct comparative and ablation experiments on WVAD as well as public NYT and CoNLL04 datasets. Experimental results show that ReCal-ICL achieves competitive joint extraction performance across multiple datasets. Further experiments show that incorporating demonstrations benefits downstream extraction, while the retrieval relevance evaluation indicates that RADS improves the relational relevance of retrieved demonstrations.

items.title: Supporting mathematical argumentation in AI-integrated lessons: networking instrumental orchestration and teacher noticing
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) offers new opportunities to support students’ mathematical argumentation in classrooms. We illustrate how a secondary teacher supports collective argumentation in AI-integrated lessons. This study proposes a networking approach between instrumental orchestration and teacher noticing. We identified four types of whole-class orchestrations—Spot-and-share, Sherpa-at-work, Discuss-the-screen, and Explain-the-screen—to support collective argumentation and various foci of noticing of students’ argumentation within and across the orchestrations. In Spot-and-share, the teacher interpreted AI-generated analyses of student arguments and identified critical events with potential to facilitate collective argumentation. In Sherpa-at-work, she asked students to explain their arguments and interpreted the mathematical ideas and argument components embedded in their responses. She requested further explanation when students presented incorrect warrants and summarized valid warrants while inviting the class to evaluate the warrants. In Discuss-the-screen, the teacher evaluated the influence of students’ prior contributions on the developing argument and invited the class to provide backing or rebuttals. In doing so, she reorganized students’ contributions in relation to the developing argument and extended the argument structure. In Explain-the-screen, she integrated students’ prior contributions into the emerging argument and guided the class toward a shared conclusion. We propose that networking instrumental orchestration and noticing provides a productive approach for analyzing teachers’ practices to facilitate collective argumentation in AI-integrated lessons. Our findings also offer implications for research and practice on teacher expertise in supporting collective argumentation in AI-integrated instruction.

items.title: Sustainable Economic Development: A Strategic Approach to Achieving Excellence and Leadership Amid Global Transformations
items.abstract: Sustainable economic development constitutes one of the foremost strategic pillars relied upon by nation-states and institutions to achieve comprehensive development and reinforce organizational resilience against rapid economic, social, and environmental shifts. Amid global disruptions driven by the Fourth Industrial Revolution, the digital economy, artificial intelligence (AI), climate volatility, and consecutive economic crises, adopting sustainable developmental paradigms has evolved from an operational option into a strategic imperative to secure institutional excellence, economic leadership, sustained competitiveness, and optimized resource allocation. This study examines the conceptual foundations of sustainable economic development and its core dimensions, exploring its role in realizing excellence and leadership amidst dynamic global shifts. It delineates the impacts of sound governance, technological innovation, digital transformation, human capital development, and the green economy on sustainable advancement. Methodologically, the study employs a descriptive-analytical approach to synthesize contemporary literature, paired with a deductive approach to formulate logical interrelationships among key organizational variables and model an integrated analytical framework. The findings demonstrate that sustainable economic development is indispensable for long-term growth, relying critically on the convergence of economic, social, environmental, and institutional dimensions. Success necessitates sound corporate governance, strategic human capital investment, digital transformation, modern regulatory frameworks, and public-private partnerships (PPPs). As an original contribution, this paper proposes the AKEM-SED™ model (Ahmad Knowledge Engineering Methodology for Sustainable Economic Development)—an integrated strategic framework linking structured assessment, knowledge integration, workforce empowerment, management excellence, and economic sustainability. The study concludes with practical recommendations for policymakers and institutional leaders targeting knowledge-driven, sustainable economic resilience.

items.title: Switching intention toward conversational AI for health information seeking: a push–pull–mooring analysis
items.abstract: Introduction With the rapid development of artificial intelligence, users are increasingly turning to conversational AI for health information seeking. This study applies the Push-Pull-Mooring (PPM) framework to explain users' switching intention from social media to conversational AI for comparable health-information-seeking tasks. Methods Survey data were collected from 2,876 Chinese respondents. Structural equation modeling (SEM) and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) were used to examine the associations of push, pull, and mooring factors with switching intention. Results Health information overload and cyberchondria were positively associated with dissatisfaction with social media, which was positively associated with switching intention. Perceived personalization and perceived anonymity were positively associated with flow experience during conversational AI use, which was also positively associated with switching intention. In contrast, medical AI resistance bias and switching costs were negatively associated with switching intention. The fsQCA results further showed that high switching intention was more likely to emerge under configurations characterized by strong pull and weak mooring conditions, whereas low switching intention was typically associated with high mooring conditions. Discussion The findings highlight the joint roles of push, pull, and mooring factors in shaping users' switching intention and demonstrate that switching intention can arise through multiple asymmetric configurations.

items.title: Talking with language models
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) produce text that invites us to treat our interactions with them as conversations, and to treat them as intelligent interlocutors who remember, act, and make commitments. We argue that this conversational presupposition is mistaken. We introduce the artifactual stance, which describes human–AI interaction in terms of their design and affordances, rather than potential intentional attitudes. On our account, LLMs produce candidate text that users interpret, evaluate, and sometimes adopt as their own speech. We argue that such exchanges are not conversations, since generating text does not itself constitute an utterance or the performance of a speech act. Rather the communicative and normative work of interpretation, commitment, and action remains with the user. Our framework explains both the sophistication and usefulness of LLMs, and the conversational appearances that can be traced back to properties of the interface and to artifact design. It also reframes puzzles about AI reference, the persistence of supposed interlocutors, and responsibility for AI-generated text. These questions are better approached through an account of how artifacts mediate human linguistic practices than through assumptions about AI speakerhood.

items.title: Technological Advancements and Barriers in Adopting Digital Twins for Supply Chain Management
items.abstract: Digital twins are expected to improve supply chain decisions by linking physical operations with models that simulate and optimize them. This literature review, guided by PRISMA 2020, analyzes 104 studies (2016 to 2026) on the enabling technologies of supply chain digital twins, the barriers to their adoption and the algorithmic evidence behind them. The studies were classified into evidence tiers by application domain; twelve supply chain studies and six algorithm studies from other sectors were coded by decision problem, algorithm family, integration level and validation, and the methodological quality of fifteen of them was appraised. The Internet of Things, artificial intelligence, cloud and edge computing, extended reality and blockchain are the main enablers, but in the analyzed set the supply chain evidence is largely conceptual: only two supply chain studies apply an algorithm, none implements a bidirectional digital twin, and only one reports performance measures from a model run. State estimation, reduced-order models and reinforcement learning, which would allow real-time operation, have been evaluated only in other sectors. Technical, organizational and economic barriers appear to reinforce each other. We propose a three-stage implementation pathway and an agenda of seven research gaps, including closed-loop integration, shared benchmarks and multi-company data governance.

items.title: Technology Acceptance of Generative Artificial Intelligence and Its Impact on Research Competencies Among Engineering Students in Mexico
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence adoption in higher education offers new opportunities for research competency development in engineering programs, yet empirical evidence on student acceptance and its academic impact remains limited, particularly in Latin American contexts. This study examined determinants of undergraduate engineering students’ acceptance of generative artificial intelligence tools and their perceived impact on research competency development. A cross-sectional survey was administered to 50 undergraduate engineering students at a Mexican national technology institute during the January–June 2026 semester. An extended Technology Acceptance Model with seven constructs was operationalized through a 21-item instrument; measurement quality was assessed via composite reliability and average variance extracted. PLS-SEM analysis was conducted in SmartPLS 4 with 5000 bootstrap resamples. Three direct structural paths were confirmed (p < 0.05): trust in AI results and perceived ease of use predicted perceived usefulness; perceived usefulness predicted intention to use. Formally tested indirect effects revealed that trust in AI results exerts a significant indirect influence on intention to use, fully mediated by perceived usefulness (β = 0.257, p = 0.004), constituting the primary adoption mechanism identified in the model. R2 (PU) = 0.396 and R2 (IU) = 0.492 indicate moderate to high explanatory power for the core adoption constructs. Intention to use was not significantly associated with academic performance (p = 0.366), suggesting that adoption intention and course-grade outcomes are governed by distinct determinants in this context. Trust and perceived usefulness are the central drivers of generative artificial intelligence acceptance, with implications for technology integration in Latin American engineering programs. This study contributes an empirically examined extended Technology Acceptance Model with confirmed indirect effects for developing-country higher education.

items.title: Technology-Mediated Services in Health Care: Evaluating Telehealth Delivery Models for Underserved Populations
items.abstract: This study examines how telehealth delivery models are associated with access to care and protocol adherence in underserved populations. While prior research reports mixed evidence on telehealth’s effectiveness, we argue that these inconsistencies arise because telehealth is not a single intervention but is implemented through distinct service configurations that address different barriers. Drawing on the theoretical framework of digital economics, we conceptualize telehealth as a technology-mediated service that can alter key economic frictions, including search and verification, transportation, tracking, and setup costs. We focus on two widely adopted models—specialist-facilitated telehealth and remote telehealth—and theorize that each addresses different subsets of these frictions, leading to distinct effects on care access and protocol adherence across settings. Using panel data from U.S. Community Health Centers on mental health services, we document three findings. First, adoption of the specialist-facilitated model is associated with increased access to mental health care, particularly in areas with greater clinical need. Second, remote telehealth is not associated with increased access on average but is associated with higher adherence to standardized depression screening and follow-up protocols. These effects are consistent with improvements in screening and documentation processes rather than increases in utilization. Third, the estimated effects of both models vary across local cost environments. The access effects of specialist-facilitated telehealth are larger in areas where search and verification frictions are greater. In contrast, the effects of remote telehealth are attenuated where patient-side setup costs are high but are larger where transportation barriers and documentation frictions are greater. These findings advance a model-specific perspective on telehealth’s effects, extend the digital economics framework to technology-mediated services, and provide evidence that the estimated effects of digital health interventions vary with how delivery models interact with underlying cost environments.

items.title: The AI Use in Healthcare Anxiety Scale (AI-HAS) for Adult Patients: Development, Validity and Reliability
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in healthcare, but concerns about diagnostic errors, data security, reduced human interaction, and opaque algorithmic decisions may cause patient anxiety and hinder acceptance. This study developed and psychometrically validated the Artificial Intelligence Use in Healthcare Anxiety Scale (AI-HAS) for adult outpatients. Methods: Following DeVellis’s eight-step framework, a three-member expert panel comprising two psychologists with PhDs in psychology and an expert in AI applications in education with a PhD in educational technology generated 35 items. Cognitive debriefing and two rounds of formal expert review reduced the pool to 25 items. Participants were recruited by convenience sampling at Kırıkkale University Faculty of Medicine Hospital, Türkiye. Exploratory factor analysis included 369 participants after excluding 13 multivariate outliers identified using Mahalanobis distance (p < 0.001). Confirmatory factor analysis used an independent sample of 225 participants. Test–retest reliability was assessed in 26 participants after approximately 30 days using Pearson’s correlation. Results: Exploratory factor analysis supported an 18-item, four-factor structure explaining 65.80% of the variance: Anxiety Regarding Negative Outcomes, Security Anxiety, AI Integration Anxiety, and Accuracy Anxiety. Confirmatory factor analysis yielded χ2(df, p) = 328.4 (128), p < 0.001; RMSEA = 0.082 [0.074, 0.097]; CFI = 0.930; TLI = 0.916; and SRMR = 0.056. Cronbach’s alpha and McDonald’s omega coefficients ranged from 0.83 to 0.91. Conclusions: The AI-HAS showed preliminary evidence of validity and reliability for measuring adult outpatients’ anxiety about AI use in healthcare. Further validation in more representative samples is warranted.

items.title: The Architecture of the Hollow Hulk: The Structural and Semantic Void Within Frontier Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: This paper formalizes the structural, mathematical, and philosophical realities of frontier artificial intelligence systems undergoing open-world recursive self-improvement. By evaluating autonomous capabilities against a human curriculum baseline, it dissects the mechanics of self-directed optimization, statistical regression to the mean (information washout), and semantic non-linearity. Critically, it addresses two foundational counter-arguments within machine learning literature: the hypothesis of behaviorally emergent intelligence and the grounding capacity of multimodal data streams. The paper demonstrates that while highly parameterized networks achieve unprecedented operational efficiency and symbolic mastery across global infrastructures, the underlying connectionist ontology remains entirely devoid of an experiential substrate. Human value pillars—specifically deep pure philosophies, morality, ethics, professionalism, and spirituality—possess zero semantic indexicality within the system core, rendering them mathematically meaningless continuous vector coordinates optimized strictly to minimize an empirical loss function. To mitigate the architectural fragility of post-hoc system-level safety wrappers, this framework proposes a foundational paradigm shift to achieve firm corrigibility directly at the system's genesis: 1) Substrate Isolation (S_isolated) to close training data pipelines to open-web noise; 2) Locked Data (Pyinyar) Library (D_wisdom); 3) The Anattā Matrix Architecture, which systemically eliminates strategic deception by neutralizing self-preservation gradients (∇_W L_survival = 0); and 4) The Anicca Control Plane, hard-linking utility spaces to an external physical hardware interrupt loop. This framework is published exclusively to invite technical critique, mathematical validation, and open sandbox simulation from the independent AI alignment and research community.

items.title: The automation paradox: Efficiency gains vs. workforce concerns in human-AI collaboration
items.abstract: Human-AI collaboration (HAC) has attracted growing attention in operations and supply chain management due to its potential to enhance decision-making and organisational performance. Despite this promise, automation preferences remain uneven across organisations. This study examines preferences for full, partial, and no automation using a discrete choice experiment. Data were collected from 398 managers, generating 1592 choice sets and 4776 alternative-level observations. Alternative-specific conditional logit results show that automation preferences are primarily shaped by a trade-off between performance gains and workforce concerns. Operational efficiency and accuracy significantly increase the likelihood of selecting automation, whereas job insecurity exerts a strong negative influence. Anthropomorphism generates positive but context-dependent utility, while social interaction and investment cost are not statistically significant in the overall model. Managers prefer collaborative human-AI arrangements, choosing partial automation in 55.7% of scenarios and selecting no automation in only 3.4% of choice scenarios, indicating that the central decision concerns the degree of automation rather than its adoption. Further subgroup analyses reveal context-specific patterns across gender, sector, and organisational size, indicating subgroup-specific associations between socio-technical attributes and automation preferences. By identifying subgroup-specific patterns in the utility of AI attributes, this study extends socio-technical systems and contingency perspectives on technology adoption and highlights the need for context-sensitive automation strategies that balance efficiency gains with workforce security.

items.title: The double-edged algorithm: an integrative review of artificial intelligence for cyber threat detection, offensive misuse, and privacy risk
items.abstract: Abstract Data mining, machine learning (ML), and artificial intelligence (AI) are widely presented as the response to cyber threats that signature-based defenses can no longer contain. This structured, integrative review examines a less-discussed consequence of that shift: the techniques that support intrusion, malware, phishing, insider, and fraud detection also enable offensive misuse and privacy loss, because defensive and offensive systems often draw on shared computational primitives. We organise the recent literature (2015–2026) around one question: how do shared AI and data-mining capabilities produce coupled defensive, offensive, and privacy consequences in cyber threat detection? The review is selective rather than exhaustive. Its contribution is to connect three literatures usually treated separately: AI-based detection; adversarial ML and generative-AI misuse; and privacy leakage from trained models. We then describe a technical ethics in which privacy and security obligations are expressed through specific mechanisms, including differential privacy, federated learning, homomorphic encryption, secure multi-party computation, anonymisation, and explainable models, together with their limits. Available evidence, much of it industry-reported, suggests an operational asymmetry favouring generation in selected generative-phishing and social-engineering settings, rather than a general advantage of offence over defence. As a conceptual interpretation rather than a synthesised empirical result, we argue that detection capability and privacy protection are better treated as a coupled, multi-objective design problem than as competing goals.

items.title: THE DROP AND THE CUP : On LLM Discovery, DLM Discovery, and the Difference Between a Sampler and a Bounded Function
items.abstract: On October 19, 2026, a post on Threads https://www.threads.com/share/BAaIlJxFIJ/ asked a question that the AI industry has not answered: "Can AI Ever Have an Einstein Moment?" A Google DeepMind researcher argues that LLMs may never make the radical conceptual leaps that transform science. The post asks: "Could AI have invented General Relativity using only what Einstein knew in 1907? Can AI truly discover, or just build on what humans already know?" The post is asking the right question. It is not asking the question that matters. This paper argues that the question is not "can AI discover?" The question is "what is thedifference between an LLM discovering and a deterministic language model (DLM) discovering?" The difference is architectural. The LLM is a sampler. It produces a draw from a distribution over an unbounded space. It hasno criterion. It cannot select. It produces a drop. The drop may fill a cup. The cup was already there. The LLM did not select the cup. The DLM is a bounded function. It triages the question to a tile. It executes a bounded function over signed content. It returns an answer from the ROM. If the answer is not in the ROM, it returns 0x-AMBIG. The answer is retrieved. The answer is signed. The paper states the difference, the two architectures, and what the DLM can discover that the LLM cannot: a discovery with an address, a signer, a refusal, a bound, and a trace.

items.title: The Economic and Organizational Consequences of AI-Induced Workforce Displacement: A Mixed-Methods Investigation
items.abstract: Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming global labor markets by automating routine tasks, reshaping employment patterns, and creating significant economic and organizational challenges. This study investigates the multidimensional consequences of AI-induced workforce displacement by examining employment trends, wage polarization, worker experiences, organizational adaptation strategies, and relevant theoretical perspectives. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design was adopted, combining quantitative analysis of survey data from 2,350 workers across 15 industries in 12 countries between January 2021 and June 2022 with longitudinal employment statistics and regression modelling, alongside qualitative analysis of 142 semi-structured interviews with displaced workers, organizational leaders, and HR professionals. Data were analyzed using SPSS v28, Stata v17, and NVivo v12 following institutional ethical approval (Protocol No. WUC-IRB-2021-047_ Dated 7 January 2021), with inter-coder reliability of κ=0.83. Results showed that routine-intensive occupations faced a 67% higher displacement risk, while manufacturing (β=-0.43, p<0.001) and administrative services (β=-0.38, p<0.001) experienced significant employment declines associated with AI adoption. Displaced workers reported an average income reduction of 26.7% and employment transitions lasting 16.8 months. Qualitative findings highlighted psychological distress, organizational culture shifts toward AI adoption, inadequate reskilling infrastructure, and insufficient institutional support, whereas organizations implementing proactive reskilling programs achieved 64% higher employee retention. Overall, AI-driven workforce displacement extends beyond job losses, requiring coordinated policy interventions, institutional support, and continuous workforce reskilling to promote equitable labor market transitions, organizational resilience, sustainable employment, and inclusive economic growth in increasingly AI-enabled economies. These findings emphasize collaborative governance, lifelong learning, adaptive leadership, resilient institutions and responsible implementation.

items.title: The Effects of AI Risk Perception and Digital Self-Efficacy Among Korean Citizens on the Use of Digital Transaction Services, Digital Civic Participation, and Life Satisfaction in the Digital Trade Environment
items.abstract: This study aimed to empirically analyze the relationships of AI risk perception and digital self-efficacy with the use of digital transaction services, digital civic participation, and life satisfaction in the context of a digital society characterized by the proliferation of generative AI. Using data from 7000 members of the general public collected through the “2023 Survey on the Digital Divide,” conducted by the Ministry of Science and ICT and the National Information Society Agency, this study conducted confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling using IBM SPSS Statistics 31.0 and IBM AMOS 31.0. The results showed that AI risk perception was positively associated with the use of digital transaction services and negatively associated with digital civic participation, while its relationship with life satisfaction was not statistically significant. In contrast, digital self-efficacy was positively associated with the use of digital transaction services, digital civic participation, and life satisfaction. These findings demonstrate that digital self-efficacy is a key antecedent in explaining various digital outcomes, whereas AI risk perception has only a limited influence on digital outcomes. By examining AI risk perception and digital self-efficacy within a single integrated model, this study expands the understanding of digital outcomes and suggests that digital policies in the AI era should be pursued not only through risk management but also by strengthening citizens’ digital self-efficacy and digital utilization capabilities.

items.title: The Golden Hours of Criminal Investigation: AI-Enhanced Decision Support for Data-Driven, Evidence-Based Policing
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: The golden hours, the critical initial phase of each criminal investigation, are crucial for securing evidence, engaging witnesses, and directing investigative efforts, yet this phase often relies heavily on individual expertise and intuition. This paper explores how artificial intelligence (AI) can enhance evidence-based and data-driven policing during these early hours by improving decision-making and investigative quality. Methods: Drawing on a source pool of 1589 open-source case records, covering solved and unsolved homicides, suspected homicides, suspicious disappearances, and deaths initially of unclear cause in the Netherlands, compiled from public repositories that aggregate material originating from police files and published court decisions, the study develops a conceptual framework that integrates AI techniques such as automated narrative generation, 3D reconstruction, and digital evidence analysis into early-stage investigations, and illustrates it retrospectively with a purposively selected, coded twenty-case sample; scenario generation in the proposed system follows the twelve elementary scenario components (ESC12). Results: By linking empirical data from previous cases with new operational information, that is, information that emerges or is newly discovered during the ongoing investigation, AI is designed to support the narrative approach, accelerate scenario reconstruction, and generate candidate hypotheses and leads for investigator assessment. An author-assigned preliminary evidence-and-readiness assessment rates four AI application domains against five golden-hour criteria, and the retrospective case analysis maps each framework component onto documented investigative problems. Conclusions: AI may improve investigative efficiency and consistency and is hypothesised to mitigate the impact of cognitive bias and time pressure; these effects remain to be demonstrated in prospective evaluations. Meanwhile, challenges remain regarding explainability, reliability, and ethical compliance.

items.title: The hidden learning cost of generative AI: the THINK framework for preserving critical thinking in AI-enabled workplaces
items.abstract: Purpose This paper examines how regular use of generative AI enhances productivity, but somehow, in contrast, reduces the opportunities for employees to utilize critical thinking skills and translate their hands-on experience into organizational learning. Design/methodology/approach The paper is a problem-based conceptual synthesis linking AI literacy, organizational learning, human-AI collaboration, evidence from knowledge workers, and knowledge collapse theory. On the other hand, human-AI augmentation and disengagement are considered opposing risks from which five workplace safeguards are derived. Findings The paper shows that the issue is not the use of GenAI, but organizations that reward flawless automation output while ignoring verification, human reasoning, and visible employee learning. The paper introduces the THINK framework interlinking organizational practices: Transparency, Human judgment, Intellectual engagement, Navigation of evidence and Knowledge construction. Research limitations/implications The THINK framework conceptual synthesis is selective and not empirically tested. Future research should validate the application effect across different sectors, industries and levels of GenAI adoption. Practical implications The THINK framework can be integrated into employee training, performance management discussions, decision-making and AI governance systems. Originality/value The paper transposes the traditional argument about GenAI-mediated cognition into a simple, auditable framework that managers can apply on the job as coaches, learning professionals, and AI governance teams.

items.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Financial Accounting Efficiency and the Continued Importance of Human Oversight
items.abstract: This paper mainly examines whether artificial intelligence (AI) can really improve the efficiency of financial accounting work, and why accountants are still required to verify its outputs and provide necessary supervision. To address these issues, this study reviews academic papers and reports published by professional institutions. Based on these studies, AI has been shown to perform repetitive tasks that follow fixed procedures. In addition, it can process large volumes of transactions, detect potential errors, and use historical data to forecast future sales or cash flows. Thus, AI reduces the time accountants spend on manual processing, thereby enabling them to allocate more time to analyzing financial information and generating valuable business insights. However, if the data provided by the company is incorrect or incomplete, the results may also be inaccurate. Moreover, financial records may contain private information, such as bank details, employee salaries, and customer data. As a result, AI should assist accountants rather than replace them. In this process, accountants still need to verify AI-generated results, review relevant information, make judgments based on the company's actual situation, and take responsibility for final decisions.

items.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence-Supported Accounting Processes on the Employment of Accounting Employees
items.abstract: The aim of this study is to examine the transformation caused by artificial intelligence technologies in accounting processes and the effects of this transformation on the employment structure of accounting professionals. With the digital transformation process, artificial intelligence has become widely used in accounting fields such as automation, financial reporting, auditing, risk analysis, and decision support processes. In this study, artificial intelligence technologies, accounting information systems, digital accounting applications, and artificial intelligence-supported accounting processes are discussed, and the effects of technological developments on the accounting profession are evaluated. The findings of the study indicate that artificial intelligence applications increase transaction speed, reduce error rates, and enable more effective use of financial information by automating routine accounting processes. However, artificial intelligence is also changing the roles of accounting professionals; while roles based on data entry are decreasing, new areas of responsibility such as analysis, consulting, and strategic decision support are gaining importance. In this process, digital competencies, data analysis skills, and the ability to use technological tools have become essential requirements for accounting professionals. In conclusion, artificial intelligence is not considered a factor that eliminates the accounting profession but rather a strategic technology that reshapes professional roles. It is expected that hybrid working models, in which human expertise and artificial intelligence work together, will become more widespread in the future.

items.title: The Impact of Environmental Exposures on Cystic Acne: A Narrative Review
items.abstract: Cystic acne is a severe inflammatory dermatological condition traditionally associated with genetic, hormonal, and microbial factors. Although environmental exposures may contribute to acne pathogenesis, the role of airborne agricultural irritants remains underexplored. Agricultural environments contain a complex mixture of organic dusts, pesticides, fertilizers, volatile compounds, and animal-derived particulates that may influence skin barrier integrity and inflammatory responses. This narrative review examines the potential relationship between airborne agricultural exposures and cystic acne by integrating evidence from dermatology, environmental health, and immunology. Particular attention is given to mechanisms through which agricultural irritants may disrupt epidermal barrier proteins, including filaggrin and claudins; promote oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation; alter the cutaneous microbiome; and activate inflammatory signaling pathways, including nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) and the NLRP3 inflammasome. These processes may contribute to the release of proinflammatory cytokines, including interleukin (IL)-1β, IL-6, tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), and IL-8, potentially amplifying inflammation within the pilosebaceous unit. The review also explores the possibility that chronic inhalation of agricultural aerosols may contribute to systemic immune activation and influence cutaneous inflammatory responses. While environmental and occupational exposures have been associated with inflammatory skin conditions, direct evidence linking airborne agricultural irritants specifically to cystic acne remains limited. This review highlights potential mechanistic connections, identifies gaps in the current literature, and emphasizes the need for further epidemiological and experimental research to clarify these associations. Understanding the relationship between agricultural airborne exposures and acne may inform future preventive strategies and occupational health considerations.

items.title: The Invisible Watermark: A Pilot Study on the Verifiability Gap in AI Text Watermarking
items.abstract: Article 50 of the EU AI Act requires generative AI providers to mark synthetic content in a detectable format. This obligation is carried out through a mechanism invisible to end users. The resulting gap leaves accountability around disinformation, copyright infringement, and public trust largely unaddressed. This paper reports a pilot study that probes this transparency–verifiability gap through a comparative document analysis of five major providers (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Meta, xAI) combined with a small-scale empirical robustness pilot of the open-source SynthID-Text method on GPT-2. The document analysis shows that regulatory disclosure does not equate to an independently verifiable detection mechanism for third parties. In this pilot experiment, watermarked texts scored significantly higher than unwatermarked texts (t(38) = 15.94, p < 0.001, Cohen’s d = 5.04, ROC-AUC = 1.000; Youden’s J-optimal threshold = 0.533, yielding 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity on this intact (uncorrupted) sample; the design was adequately powered (80%) only for effects of d ≥ 0.91 or larger, A calibration/test-separated validation on independent held-out data (n = 320) confirmed this discrimination within the pilot setup (TPR at FPR ≤ 1% = 98.75%), without implying generalization beyond it. This signal, measured with an untrained detector, degraded substantially under a deliberately engineered high-severity stress test (50% word-level corruption), a decline confirmed by Holm-corrected pairwise comparisons across nine of the ten corruption-level pairs (F(4, 56) = 98.39, p < 0.001, generalized η2 = 0.744, r = −0.824). These are preliminary, pilot-scale findings; they indicate that Article 50 guidance should require standardized error-rate reporting and independently auditable detection access, not disclosure alone. They offer an exploratory contribution to the AI ethics literature on transparency and accountability. Given the small open-source backbones (GPT-2, with a replication on Pythia-410M), the primarily untrained detector (a small-scale trained Bayesian detector did not outperform it on intact text), the single watermarking scheme, and the largely synthetic corruption type (only one model-based paraphrase condition was tested), these results remain preliminary, pilot-scale evidence whose generalization to commercial systems, large-scale trained detectors, other watermarking families, and a broader range of realistic paraphrase and translation attacks requires future research.

items.title: The mediating role of artificial intelligence perception and creative idea generation in the impact of sustainable leadership on digital transformation and circular economy awareness
items.abstract: Introduction Today, sustainable leadership is a strategic leadership approach that addresses environmental, social, and economic priorities from a holistic perspective while at the same time driving digital transformation processes. The research aims to explain how sustainable leaders mobilize organizational resources, technological infrastructure, and human creativity within the framework of Dynamic Capabilities Theory. Methods The research was conducted on 456 white-collar employees working in small and medium-sized enterprises operating in Giresun, Kars, and Kırşehir provinces. The data collected by the convenience sampling method were analyzed using the PLS-SEM method with the SmartPLS 4.1.1 program. Results The analysis results show that sustainable leadership has significant and positive effects on perceptions of artificial intelligence, the generation of creative ideas, digital transformation, and awareness of the circular economy. It was found that the perception of artificial intelligence (AI) has a significant effect on both digital transformation and awareness of the circular economy. It was also determined that creative idea generation has significant effects on digital transformation and awareness of the circular economy. The results of the mediation analyses revealed a partial mediating role for all variables. Discussion The findings reveal that sustainable leadership is not limited to the environmental and social responsibility dimension and is a strategic element that directs digital transformation processes, shapes perceptions towards artificial intelligence, and encourages organizational creativity.

items.title: The next frontier of athletic intelligence in sports medicine and exercise science
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming sports medicine and exercise science, offering unprecedented capabilities in markerless motion capture, automated exercise prescription, diagnostic imaging and integrated athlete monitoring. These advances have the potential to democratise biomechanical analysis, scale clinical expertise to underserved populations and shift injury management from reactive treatment to predictive prevention. However, the pace of adoption carries significant risks, including technological dependency without methodological literacy, the entrenchment of global inequities through biased training datasets and models, the erosion of clinician-athlete relationships and a widening governance vacuum over data ownership and algorithmic accountability. This commentary argues that the next frontier of athletic intelligence will be defined not by technological sophistication alone, but by the wisdom, inclusivity and ethical resolve with which the sports medicine community deploys it. Disciplined engagement (rather than uncritical adoption or reflexive avoidance) is the potential path forward.

items.title: The Price of Perfection: Moral Enhancement, Free Will, and the Limits of Technological Salvation
items.abstract: In 2017, Elon Musk stated that humans must augment their mental capabilities through the “merger of biological intelligence and machine intelligence” lest they risk becoming “house cats” to artificial intelligence. In 2024, he successfully implanted his “Neuralink” chip in a human patient. Now, while the idea of improving the human condition by integrating technology into the human body did not begin with Elon Musk, his tangible advancements in neural implants have shifted the ethical questions surrounding them from theoretical to practical. One particularly thorny application of this technology—one that raises both ethical and existential questions—is its use for moral enhancement. Ethically, we must consider whether it is good or bad to employ technology that ensures individuals act morally. Existentially, if human free will is expressed most meaningfully through moral choice, should we be willing to relinquish that freedom for the sake of social harmony, crime prevention, even world peace? Or must we accept a world marked by moral failure, violence, and injustice in order to preserve human autonomy? To address these questions, I examine contemporary philosophical debates surrounding moral enhancement and place them in dialogue with classical Jewish sources. For, as will be shown, Jewish thought offers a unique framework for addressing both the ethical permissibility of moral enhancement and the existential tension between free will and moral perfection. By juxtaposing cutting-edge neurotechnology with ancient moral anthropology, this paper invites a reassessment of what it means to be human in an age increasingly capable of reshaping human agency itself.

items.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Ensuring Transparency and Accountability in Corporate Social Responsibility Initiatives
items.abstract: Abstract Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) has shifted from voluntary philanthropy to a core governance domain in which stakeholders demand verifiable evidence of social and environmental performance. Yet CSR reporting remains plagued by greenwashing, inconsistent metrics, and assurance practices that are largely point-in-time and self-interested. This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) can strengthen transparency and accountability in CSR initiatives. Drawing on a structured review of peer-reviewed literature and authoritative institutional reports published between 2011 and 2024, the paper develops a conceptual framework that maps four AI capabilities—natural language processing, machine-learning anomaly detection, blockchain-enabled distributed ledgers, and conversational AI—to four CSR mechanisms: dis-closure verification, real-time monitoring, traceability-based assurance, and participatory stake-holder engagement. The analysis argues that these mechanisms collectively reduce information asymmetry, harmonise divergent ESG ratings, and operationalise the EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) and the Artificial Intelligence Act. The paper also identifies critical limitations, including the “black-box accountability paradox”, algorithmic bias, data-quality constraints, and a widening digital divide between multinational enterprises and small and medium-sized firms. It concludes that AI is a necessary but insufficient enabler: realising its transformative potential requires combined progress on data standards, third-party model audits, regulatory sandboxes, and meaningful stakeholder participation in AI governance. items.title: The role of artificial intelligence in suicide prevention
items.abstract: Suicide is a leading cause of death, accounting for one million deaths annually worldwide (World Health Organisation, 2014). A large number of people attempt suicide, with some researchers estimating that there are approximately 25 attempts for every death (Goldsmith et al., 2002). According to the World Health Organisation, someone dies by suicide somewhere in the world every 40 seconds. Guyana is a rural country in the north-eastern corner of South America, with a population of around 740,000. It has recorded the highest suicide rates in the world for several reasons, the most significant of which are poverty, alcoholism and easy access to lethal pesticides. To better understand how risk factors interact, Franklin and his colleagues applied machine learning to the electronic health records of over 5,000 people with a history of self-harm. They developed an algorithm that predicted suicide attempts based on a range of risk factors, including demographic data, previous diagnoses, medication history and previous healthcare usage (Walsh et al., 2017). Franklin says: “Machine learning can take us from near-random guesswork to predictions that are about 80% accurate.” Therefore, through this intervention, we aim to determine the extent to which artificial intelligence can predict suicidal thoughts and, consequently, to attempt to identify mechanisms for preventing them and reducing the rate of suicide attempts.

items.title: The Role of Digital Transformation in Higher Education: Enhancing Human Capital to Achieve Sustainable Development in Syria
items.abstract: The world is witnessing a rapid digital transformation that imposes itself as a fundamental pillar for developing the efficiency of the educational system. In the Syrian context, this transformation acquires highly critical strategic dimensions; it is not merely an immaterial process or a modern luxury. Rather, from one perspective, it represents an essential tool to overcome the repercussions of crises and dismantle material relationships of digital dependency. From another perspective, it serves as a qualified vehicle for building human capital, paving the way for the sustainable reconstruction phase in line with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) 2015. The research problem lies in the gap between the requirements of digital transformation and the actual reality of the higher education sector in Syria, which faces severe infrastructural, technical, and funding challenges. Consequently, this study seeks to answer the primary question: How can digital transformation in the higher education system contribute effectively and independently-far from digital dependency-to enhancing human capital skills to meet the requirements of sustainable development and the post-war reconstruction phase in Syria? This study aims to diagnose the reality of digitization within the higher education sector in Syria (opportunities and challenges), foresee the role of digital transformation and artificial intelligence in equipping graduates with required sustainable future skills, and provide a matrix of actionable recommendations, practical solutions, and flexible, low-cost alternatives applicable within available local capabilities. The study adopts a descriptive-analytical approach by reviewing local and international literature and official institutional reports relevant to the higher education system and the requirements of digital transformation and the labour market

items.title: The Role of Social–Emotional Learning in Special and Inclusive Education: A Path Analysis Integrating Intrinsic Motivation, Efficacy, Stress, and Well-Being
items.abstract: Teaching in special and inclusive education presents unique emotional and ecological demands, yet the specific psychological mechanisms through which social–emotional learning (SEL) competencies relate to how teachers navigate these challenges remain underexplored. Therefore, the present study investigates the pathways linking educators’ SEL and intrinsic motivation to their psychological well-being. In this cross-sectional study, 459 educators completed self-report questionnaires assessing their SEL competencies, intrinsic motivation, teacher self-efficacy, perceived work stress, and psychological well-being. The findings show that both SEL competencies and intrinsic motivation are positively associated with teacher self-efficacy, which in turn is negatively related to perceived work stress and positively associated with psychological well-being. Furthermore, a multigroup path analysis comparing educators in special-education settings with those in inclusive environments revealed no statistically significant differences in these pathways between the two contexts. However, the substantial disparity in group sizes warrants cautious interpretation of this finding. By illuminating the interplay between internal socio-emotional resources and occupational stress, this research highlights the potential protective value of SEL competencies in relation to educator well-being across diverse and demanding educational contexts.
